title: A Touch Is Not a Fusion

scenes.visual: Title card: A Touch Is Not a Fusion. Show separate neuron outlines linked at specialized contacts.

scenes.tts: In the vertebrate nervous system, neurons are separate cells. Each has its own membrane. They pass signals across specialized contacts, rather than forming one fused net. That is the neuron doctrine. It matters because development has to wire cells together. And we can trace the direction of signal flow from cell to cell. Two fine nerve branches meet. Their contact connects separate cells.

scenes.visual: Begin with blue and yellow neurons, each enclosed by its own membrane. Highlight their specialized contact without merging the outlines. Show a circuit of separate cells and arrows for signal flow. End on the meeting branches; keep the separate-cell answer visible.

scenes.tts: Development gave evidence for this view. Wilhelm His argued that each nerve fibre grows out from a single young cell, a neuroblast. Cajal described growth cones at the tips of young axons in chick embryos. He read them as advancing ends of growing fibres. Cajal's specimens were fixed and dead. Movement was an inference from still shapes.

scenes.visual: Show a nerve fibre extending from one neuroblast in a schematic. Then show fixed chick-embryo axon tips with cone-shaped and fringed endings. Label the historical specimens as fixed; use successive still drawings to convey inferred growth, not live observation.

scenes.tts: Separate cells also have a usual direction of signal flow. Signals enter through dendrites and the cell body, and leave through the axon. This is dynamic polarization. It helps explain one-way signalling through a chain of cells. It is a useful generalization, with exceptions, including synapses between dendrites.

scenes.visual: Label dendrites, cell body and axon on a neuron. Animate arrows along a chain of separate neurons in the usual direction. Briefly show a dendrite-to-dendrite contact as an exception; do not depict the generalization as universal.

scenes.tts: How could anyone follow a cell in crowded tissue? Golgi's black reaction fills a few neurons completely, while most stay pale. A single cell and its branches stand out, though branches leaving the section are cut off. Golgi read fine axon branches as a continuous net. Cajal found branches ending near other cells without joining them.

scenes.visual: Show crowded tissue, then a few fully stained neurons against pale neighbours. Trace one cell and its branches, marking where branches are cut at the section edge. Compare Golgi's inferred axon network with Cajal's free endings. Label these as interpretations.

scenes.tts: The light microscope could not settle the disagreement. Fine branches touching, or passing close at different depths in a thick section, could look the same. The image could not tell contact from fusion.

scenes.visual: Cover the junction with the red historical light-microscope resolution disc. Compare touching branches with branches at different depths that overlap in projection. Label the view as unresolved.

scenes.tts: The direct test came in the nineteen fifties. Electron microscopy showed two separate membranes at chemical synapses, with a narrow cleft between them and small vesicles in the terminal. The gap was visible at last. Separate cells form circuits through specialized contacts.

scenes.visual: Zoom from the unresolved junction to a chemical synapse with two distinct membranes, a cleft and vesicles in the terminal. Label the electron-microscopy evidence and pull back to the circuit of separate cells.

scenes.tts: A smaller point: electrical synapses couple some neurons through channels that pass ions and small molecules. The channels can close. Each neuron still keeps its own membrane.

scenes.visual: Label this closing scene A smaller point: electrical coupling. Show channels between two distinct membranes passing ions and small molecules, then closing. Keep each cell's membrane outline visible.
End card with a chain of separate neurons linked at specialized contacts. Text: Separate cells form circuits.
